patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral ptosis, dysarthria, and dysphagia worse in afternoons — also has chronic skin rash
patient.hpi:
A 69-year-old Indian man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a chronic violaceous pruritic skin eruption on the extremities (diagnosed one year earlier as lichen planus by dermatology) presented to the neurology ward with a 20-day history of mild bilateral ptosis, dysarthria, and progressive dysphagia. Dysarthria developed first — a nasal quality to his speech that his wife noticed was more pronounced by evening — followed within 3 days by difficulty swallowing solids that progressed over the next week to difficulty with liquids. He noted that symptoms were consistently and markedly better in the morning upon waking and significantly worsened through the afternoon and evening. He denied diplopia, headache, vertigo, dizziness, shortness of breath, or limb weakness.

He had no recent infections, travel, or significant dietary changes. His family history was unremarkable for neuromuscular disease. On physical examination, he was afebrile with normal vital signs. Dermatologic examination confirmed flat-topped violaceous papules on the flexural surfaces of both lower extremities with overlying hyperpigmented macules — characteristic lichen planus morphology. Neurological examination demonstrated asymmetric bilateral ptosis (left greater than right) without ophthalmoplegia. Gag reflex was severely reduced. Palate elevation was symmetric but weak. Tongue movements were intact with no fasciculations or atrophy. Proximal muscle strength was 5/5 with clinically apparent fatigability on sustained resistance testing. Reflexes were 2+ symmetric. Sensation was intact throughout.
pmh: Lichen planus (skin), diagnosed 1 year ago by dermatology

family_history: Father had hypertension; no neuromuscular disease

social_history.note: Retired civil servant; non-smoker; occasional alcohol; lives with wife; community college part-time lecturer

physical_exam.general: Alert, cooperative; bilateral ptosis visible; skin rash visible on bilateral lower extremities
physical_exam.neurological: Asymmetric bilateral ptosis (left > right) without ophthalmoplegia. Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze. Cogan lid twitch positive. Severe reduction of gag reflex. Palate elevation: symmetric but weak. No tongue deviation or fasciculations. Proximal limb strength 5/5 with clear fatigability on sustained resistance. DTR 2+ symmetric. Sensation intact. Coordination normal. Gait normal.
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs
physical_exam.extremities: Violaceous papules and hyperpigmented macules on bilateral lower extremity flexures — lichen planus morphology

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: AChR antibody–positive generalized myasthenia gravis (G70.01) — late-onset with lichen planus autoimmune background

differential.key_features: Normal needle EMG (no fasciculations or denervation); fatigable pattern with diurnal variation (not ALS); AChR antibody positive
No 50 Hz increment; ptosis and bulbar symptoms predominant (not proximal limb-predominant); no SCLC on CT
differential.distinguishing_test: 50 Hz RNS (no increment), anti-VGCC (negative), CT chest (normal)

differential.key_features: Normal brain MRI/DWI; diurnal variation and fatigability incompatible with fixed vascular deficit
OPMD has ptosis and dysphagia but gradual onset over decades; no fatigable component; normal RNS; genetic testing (PABPN1)
differential.distinguishing_test: RNS (abnormal in MG, normal in OPMD), PABPN1 genetic testing

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI to exclude brainstem lesion given ptosis and bulbar dysfunction
RNS with low-rate (3 Hz) in multiple muscle groups to confirm NMJ dysfunction
AChR antibody panel for serological confirmation
Initiate pyridostigmine; add prednisone with PPI; intensify diabetes monitoring

critical_actions: Recognize diurnal variation (worse in PM) as hallmark MG feature
RNS showing decremental response in 3 muscle groups is diagnostic
Order AChR antibody — result is strongly positive and confirms diagnosis
CT chest for thymoma screening in all new MG
Monitor NIF and FVC given bulbar involvement
Account for prednisone impact on T2DM glucose control
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe fluoroquinolones or aminoglycosides in this patient
Do not dismiss bulbar symptoms as lichen planus-related (not causally related)
Do not fail to adjust diabetes management when starting prednisone
key_reasoning_points: Diurnal variation with worse symptoms in the afternoon is the hallmark clinical feature distinguishing MG from ALS, stroke, and myopathy
Multi-muscle decremental response on RNS (3 sites) is electrophysiological confirmation — high specificity
Lichen planus co-diagnosis is a red herring — it is incidentally present but shares autoimmune background
Normal needle EMG (no fasciculations) effectively excludes ALS/motor neuron disease
No 50 Hz increment on RNS excludes LEMS pattern

red_herrings.finding: Lichen planus on skin exam — considered as possible paraneoplastic or connective tissue disorder
red_herrings.why_misleading: Lichen planus with bulbar dysfunction might suggest a paraneoplastic process or SLE with neurological involvement
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Lichen planus is an incidental autoimmune co-diagnosis; does not cause bulbar dysfunction; MG is the independent cause

red_herrings.why_misleading: Elevated ESR with neurological symptoms could suggest vasculitis or inflammatory condition
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-specific mild elevation; normal CRP; no other vasculitis features; attributed to mild chronic inflammation from lichen planus

red_herrings.finding: Elevated HbA1c suggesting inadequately controlled diabetes
red_herrings.why_misleading: Poorly controlled diabetes with peripheral neuropathy could cause mild bulbar dysfunction
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal nerve conduction on EMG study; T2DM at this HbA1c level would not cause fatigable bulbar weakness; RNS and AChR antibody confirm MG

metadata.condition_name: Generalized MG with late-onset presentation and incidental lichen planus
metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward: classic diurnal variation with bulbar and ocular fatigability; multi-muscle RNS decrement confirmed; lichen planus is an incidental distractor

additional_observations:
CT CHEST

Indication: Newly suspected MG; screen for thymoma

FINDINGS: No anterior mediastinal mass. Thymic involution appropriate for age. No mediastinal adenopathy. No pulmonary nodules.

IMPRESSION: Normal chest CT. No thymoma.

findings.description:
REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION STUDY

Indication: Fatigable ptosis, bulbar dysfunction; RNS for NMJ assessment

TECHNIQUE: 3 Hz RNS performed at anconeus (radial nerve), trapezius (accessory nerve), and orbicularis oculi (facial nerve)

RESULTS:
  Anconeus: Decrement 14% from 1st to 4th stimulus [>10% abnormal] ABNORMAL
  Trapezius: Decrement 16% ABNORMAL
  Orbicularis oculi: Decrement 12% ABNORMAL

MOTOR NERVE CONDUCTION: Normal distal latencies and amplitudes; no evidence of peripheral neuropathy.

SENSORY NERVE CONDUCTION: Normal.

NEEDLE EMG (distal and proximal muscles): Normal insertional activity; no fibrillations, no fasciculations; no myopathic or neuropathic motor unit morphology changes.

HIGH-RATE RNS (50 Hz): No facilitating response — LEMS pattern excluded.

INTERPRETATION: Abnormal decremental response at 3 Hz in three muscle groups (anconeus 14%, trapezius 16%, orbicularis 12%). Normal needle EMG and nerve conduction. No 50 Hz increment. Findings are diagnostic of myasthenia gravis.

CONCLUSION: Electrophysiological confirmation of generalized MG with multi-muscle decremental response.

specialized_test.impression: RNS: 14-16% decrement at anconeus, trapezius, orbicularis; normal EMG; no 50Hz increment — confirms generalized MG

findings.description:
SINGLE-FIBER EMG — ORBICULARIS OCULI

MCD: 58 µs [normal <35 µs] MARKEDLY ABNORMAL
Blocking: 20% of potential pairs

CONCLUSION: SFEMG confirms NMJ dysfunction. Consistent with MG.

output.impression: SFEMG: MCD 58 µs with 20% blocking — NMJ dysfunction confirmed

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Lichen Planus and Myasthenia Gravis Association

KEY FINDINGS:
1. POLYAUTOIMMUNE ASSOCIATIONS: Lichen planus is a T-cell–mediated immune disorder; it has been described in association with other autoimmune conditions including MG, autoimmune hepatitis, and thyroid disease
2. CASE SERIES: Small series report co-occurrence of lichen planus and MG, suggesting shared immunological susceptibility (HLA-DR1, HLA-DQ1)
3. CLINICAL IMPLICATION: Lichen planus does not cause MG and is not a diagnostic confounder; the two conditions share autoimmune background
4. STEROIDS IN BOTH: Prednisone is first-line immunosuppression for MG and can also improve lichen planus — an incidental treatment benefit

CONCLUSION: Lichen planus is an incidental autoimmune co-diagnosis; does not affect MG management.
output.summary: Lichen planus and MG can co-exist as part of polyautoimmune predisposition; prednisone treats both; no diagnostic interaction

output.report:
DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — METFORMIN + PYRIDOSTIGMINE IN MG + T2DM

Query: Drug interactions for new MG treatment in patient with T2DM on metformin

FINDINGS:
  METFORMIN + PYRIDOSTIGMINE: No clinically significant interaction
  PREDNISONE + METFORMIN: Prednisone causes significant hyperglycemia; T2DM glucose management must be intensified; consider SGLT-2 inhibitor or insulin adjustment; monitor HbA1c
  AMLODIPINE: Mild NMJ concern at high doses; continue at current 5 mg dose with monitoring

PRACTICAL NOTE: Starting prednisone in a T2DM patient requires close blood glucose monitoring. Consider endocrinology co-management. HbA1c 7.6% is already borderline — steroid-induced hyperglycemia may require additional pharmacological management.

CONCLUSION: Add PPI with prednisone; intensify diabetes monitoring; no interaction with metformin + pyridostigmine.
output.summary: Prednisone will worsen T2DM glucose control — intensify monitoring; no metformin-pyridostigmine interaction

additional_observations:
CT CHEST FOR THYMECTOMY EVALUATION (REPEAT WITH DEDICATED VIEWS)

Indication: AChR+ MG confirmed; MGTX trial evidence for thymectomy benefit in non-thymomatous generalized MG

FINDINGS: No thymoma. Fatty thymic involution. No anterior mediastinal mass. No adenopathy.

MGTX TRIAL APPLICABILITY:
  - Patient age: 69 years (MGTX included 18-65; patient is outside trial age range)
  - AChR+: Yes (qualifies on antibody criterion)
  - Age >65: MGTX evidence is extrapolated; current guidelines support thymectomy in AChR+ generalized MG even up to age 65-70 based on expert opinion
  - No thymoma: Thymectomy still beneficial for non-thymomatous MG per MGTX trial

CONCLUSION: No thymoma found. MGTX trial evidence supports thymectomy for AChR+ generalized MG; borderline age may require multidisciplinary discussion (neurology + thoracic surgery + patient preference).
output.impression: No thymoma; MGTX thymectomy benefit established for AChR+ generalized MG up to age ~65-70; discuss with patient
